Entropy’s Edge
 A Specification for a Game of Organized Structure, Costly Time, Nested Boundaries,
                         and Delayed Consequence

                                     Flyxion
                            Independent Researcher

                                October 2026


                                     Abstract
      Entropy’s Edge is a space strategy and space-flight game whose central problem is main-
      taining organized structure against the processes that dissipate it. The world is a simulated
      environment of three interacting fields, a scalar constraint density, a directional flow, and
     an entropy density, and the calendar is a resource, every boundary is a potential trigger,
     and nothing a player does to another player is visible until its consequences have had time
      to arrive. This document specifies the field substrate, the game’s time model, its world of
      nested scopes, the strategic layer of stars, corridors, fleets, factions and victory conditions,
      the visual direction, the control scheme, the global reset and its inoculations, the blink
     mechanism and its automated tiers, the placement and defusal of core triggers, the minefield
      economy, the guide bot that doubles as tutorial and screensaver, the multiplayer rules that
      follow from isolation across interstellar distances, and the status of the existing prototypes
      together with the gap that remains between them and the design. The design began as a
      response to a defect in ordinary social platforms, where a date attached to a post or a page
        is a free-form field that readers nevertheless treat as evidence. The game takes the opposite
      position: a date is a coordinate in a recorded tree of choices, every movement along the
      date axis has a price, and what one player learns about another is always an effect and
      never a claim. The document also states the rules by which events cross between the branch
       histories of different players, separates the several protections against a global reset, fixes
      the eligibility and propagation rules for core triggers, and records, with a status label for
      each, which parts of the design are recorded decisions, which are proposals made here, and
     which describe verified code.

1  Motivation and Design Stance

The immediate source of the design is an observation about how timestamps behave on a large
social platform. A page there can carry posts dated to any moment between its recorded
founding and, until limits were added, a point decades in the future. A post may be dated to
the year of the Battle of Hastings, a page may display a job at a space station on a moon of
Saturn in 1915, and an event may be scheduled for 2042 after the platform has since capped
scheduling at two years, because the cap was applied to new entries and the old ones were left
in place. The interface renders all of these in exactly the same format as a post whose date is
real. A visitor reading a long timeline therefore receives what looks like a track record, and the
platform’s own presentation lends credibility to a history that nobody checked. The same effect
arises innocently when a page is renamed: posts made under an earlier identity appear under
the current name with no seam, so an idea seems older than it is. The information that would
correct the impression, namely the creation date and the name history, exists in the system but
has been moved out of the main view.
  Two distinct clocks are being displayed through a single slot. One is the time at which
something was posted, which only the platform can know. The other is the time at which
something is said to have happened, which only the poster can claim. Because the display
does not distinguish them, the reader cannot tell a verified fact from an assertion, and because
longevity is one of the cheapest trust signals people use, the confusion is exploitable.
   Entropy’s Edge is the attempt to build a world in which the same capability is a feature
and not a flaw. Players may move along the time axis, backward as well as forward, but every
movement is priced, every movement is recorded in a tree that the player can inspect, and no
player is ever asked to believe another player’s date. The three commitments that follow from
this stance organize the rest of the specification.
Principle 1 (Dates are paid for). A change of position on the time axis costs something the
player can observe: real time, level progress, or a consumable resource. A date is therefore
evidence of what was spent to reach it.
Principle 2 (Seams are readable). Operations that revise or interrupt history leave a mark in
the player’s own record, and the game surfaces armed and hidden structure to players who have
invested in perceiving it.
Principle 3 (Effects, not claims). What reaches a player from another player is the consequence
of that other player’s choices after the signal has had time to arrive. Nothing about another
player’s present is asserted to anyone.

1.1 A second motivation: ecological proxies and collective selection
The design has a second root, which concerns money. The argument is that money behaves
as a toxic meme: by making things quantifiable and comparable it sets up an optimization
problem about acquiring more of it, which pushes people to categorize themselves and others
by wealth and distorts what they attend to, in the way the arrival of a single bottle disturbs
a moneyless society in The Gods Must Be Crazy. The reply is theory-laden, and the version
adopted here is that money is a dynamic proxy and that the proxy should be shifted toward
ecological awareness. The supporting proposals are hierarchical swarm piloting, in which the

                                         5

passengers of a vehicle each pilot local drones and identify hazards through tablets or voice,
invisible walls built from robotic animals that steer and monitor herds, and the conversion of
every city into a kelp farm and rainforest generator.
  The game is the experiment that gives these proposals a testing ground. Players try different
terraformation schemes, technology trees, and takeoff rates, and the community then collectively
selects the most coherent extrapolation. The field substrate of Section 3 is the physics of that
experiment, the resources and crystals are its currencies, and the branch tree is how many
extrapolations can be compared without being confused with one another. A further device
from the same source is the counterfoil choice, described for the Kalabari, in which an option is
offered mainly to show where a decision should not go, and Section 7 uses it for the reset key.

1.2  Conventions for status
The design draws on three kinds of record and this specification marks which is which. A
recorded decision is something the designer stated in the design discussions. A proposal is
an interpretation or a rule introduced in this document to resolve an inconsistency or fill a
gap. An implementation fact describes code that was actually inspected. Appendix A lists the
principal statements of the specification with their status, and a reader who needs to know
whether a given rule has been decided should consult it.

2  The Time Model

2.1  The calendar and its endpoints
Play begins in the year 2400. The player may advance the year, and advancing is the cheap and
default direction of travel. At the first level the passage of time is controlled by zoom: zooming
out speeds time up and zooming in slows it down, which makes time control tactile and not
a menu option. The earliest point on the axis is the Big Bang, about fourteen billion years
before the start. A global reset, described in Section 7, returns a player to that earliest point,
and the universe then unfolds back to 2400 over five minutes of real time, on a logarithmic
schedule that runs fast at first and slows until the rate reaches parity with the ordinary clock.
Backward movement short of a reset is gated: it becomes available only at the second level,
which is reached by visiting a large number of stars, and it requires time crystals, which are
a consumable and also act as a vector multiplier. The records state both that zoom changes
the speed of time at the first level and that slowing time belongs to the time crystals. This
specification reconciles the two by treating zoom as the coarse control that every player has
over how fast their own simulation advances, and the crystals as the extension of control to
direction and to fine adjustment.
  The asymmetry between directions is deliberate and is built into the interface. Most players
are expected to move forward easily and backward rarely. This mirrors the way time behaves
for everyone and gives the backward direction the scarcity that makes it informative when it is
used.




                                         6

2.2  The tree of choices
The history of a player is a branching tree, and only branches that have been chosen or created
are computed. A position on the time axis is a node in that tree, and the date displayed is
the date attached to the node. Rewinding to an earlier date selects an earlier node, and a new
choice made from there creates a new branch while the old line remains in the record. This is
the same structure a version-control system maintains, and the analogy is useful because it
makes the cost model explicit.
  Once a player’s parameter choices along a path are fixed, returning to the furthest point
along that path is nearly free. A player who has rewound can spam the year-forward key and
travel back up the existing branch with almost no effort, up to the earliest external event that
newly applies to it, as Section 10 explains. The expensive operation is divergence, that is,
making a different set of choices at an earlier node, because divergence is what creates new
history. The five-minute climb from the Big Bang is not the price of time travel as such. It is
the price of having discarded one’s accumulated position, and it falls on a player who has used
the reset rather than a rewind.

2.3  Interpolation
A player may be further along in the future than the point from which a revision is made. In
that case a revision is not an edit to the past but an interpolation: the player fills in a path
between two known endpoints, the earlier node and the later one already reached. This is a
projected inquiry, in which the player poses a hypothetical path, examines its implications, and
then commits it. The interface allows most players to go forward easily and does not allow
them to rewrite backward without this projection, so interpolation is the ordinary method by
which a recorded past is revised.
Rule 1 (Marking interpolated stretches). A segment of a player’s tree that was produced by
interpolation and not lived through step by step is displayed differently from a lived segment,
and a distant observer who eventually sees the consequences can see that the segment was
reconstructed. Interpolation is a visible feature of the record and is never presented as though it
were lived time.

2.4  Endpoints and the shape of the history
Determinism makes replay from an earlier state well defined, but it does not guarantee that a
newly chosen sequence of interventions will arrive at a later state that has already been fixed.
Connecting two prescribed endpoints is a constrained reachability problem, and the specification
must say what the later endpoint means. There are three strengths. An endpoint may be a
date only, an endpoint may be a set of constraints on the world state that the reconstructed
path must satisfy, or an endpoint may be the exact world state. This specification takes the
exact state as the default meaning of an interpolation, so that a projected inquiry can fail.
The promise the game can safely make is narrow: it tests a proposed sequence of interventions
against the endpoint and rejects any candidate that misses it. That a candidate fails does not
show that no permitted sequence succeeds, and the word infeasible is reserved for cases that a
solver can certify, by an exhaustive search of a finite space, by a proof of unreachability, or by a


                                         7

complete solver for the restricted system. Equality is taken on an explicitly defined simulation
state, which excludes provenance and node identity, since those necessarily differ between the
original endpoint and its reconstructed counterpart. A request that fixes only a date, or only
some constraints, is not an interpolation in the full sense, because the reconstructed branch
may reach the same year with a different world, and it is recorded as a fork with an explicit
marker of which constraints were kept. The distinction is the one between exact and inexact
values in a language such as Racket, where a comparison on inexact numbers can still yield an
exact result, and it serves the same purpose here: to keep what was promised separate from
what was only approximated.
  A branching history is a tree as long as every state has exactly one parent, and an interpolation
that joins two existing nodes would give a node two parents and turn the tree into a graph with
merging paths. The specification preserves the tree. An interpolated path ends at a new node
that is constrained to equal the old endpoint, and the new node carries a provenance link to the
original, so that the history of states remains a tree and the relation between a reconstructed
state and its counterpart is a recorded annotation and not a structural merge. Anyone who
prefers to allow merging may call the result a directed acyclic graph, but the replay rule and
the cost model are simpler on the tree.

2.5 Two clocks
The game keeps the two clocks that the social platform conflates. The year shown in the world
is the in-game coordinate of the player’s current node. Alongside it the game maintains a
record of how that node was reached: the jumps taken, the resets suffered, the crystals spent,
and the stretches that were interpolated. A reset is therefore a mark in the history and never
an erasure of it. A player reading their own tree can distinguish a position reached by ordinary
advance from one reached by a costly rewind.

2.6  Causal time and cosmological time
A record of provenance does not by itself supply a coordinate for scheduling, and the specification
adds one. Each branch carries a causal coordinate τ that increases monotonically along every
path of the history tree and is distinct from the displayed cosmological year Y . A reset changes
Y and selected world variables, returning the calendar to the Big Bang, and leaves τ increasing,
so that a player whose calendar has returned to the beginning has not thereby returned to an
earlier causal moment. A rewind selects an ancestor and begins a new continuation whose τ
resumes from that ancestor’s value. Signal travel, cooldowns such as the refractory period of a
retired scope, event ordering, and warning countdowns use τ, while cosmological development,
the long-term state of the fields, and the displayed calendar use Y . Events received before
a reset therefore stay received, and signals already emitted keep an unambiguous age, which
would not be so if arrivals were scheduled by a calendar that a reset can wind backward.
   Multiplayer also needs a correspondence between the causal coordinates of different players.
The engine keeps one in a global causal frame, in which each continuation segment is placed
at the moment it is created, and every delivery of an event is computed in that frame. The
correspondence is never shown to the players, and its details are left open.

3  The Field Substrate

3.1  Three fields
The strategic identity of the game was fixed in an early design discussion as a 4X game in which
players manipulate a scalar field Φ, a vector flow field v, and an entropy field S. The objective
is to sustain organized structures under a constant smoothing pressure, so that persistence, and
not accumulation, is the governing strategic problem. Exploration, colonization, production,
and conflict all operate inside this physical environment, and entropy is a working part of the
simulation and never only background lore. The scalar field Φ represents constraint density,
that is, organized structure. The vector field v represents directional flow. The entropy field S
represents the dissipation of organization. The simulation advances by three processes: diffusion,
which smooths the fields; flow reorientation, which redirects v in response to the other fields;
and dissipation, which converts organization into entropy.
  The recovered design names these processes without fixing their equations, so the form below
is offered as a candidate that respects the stated structure and leaves the coefficients open:

∂tΦ = DΦ∇2Φ−∇·(Φ v)−κ S Φ+σΦ,    ∂tS = DS∇2S−∇·(S v)+α∇∥∇Φ∥2+γ a+χ κ S Φ+σS−µSS−π,

where a is the density of operational throughput by player structures, which produces entropy
at rate γ, α∇is the rate at which gradients of organization produce entropy by relaxing, µS
is the linear damping of the prototype, σΦ and σS are player-supplied sources, π is entropy
exported by pumps into a finite external reservoir described in Section 16, and the flow v
relaxes toward a direction determined by the gradients of Φ and S plus player redirection. The
term κSΦ is the dissipation pressure that makes unmaintained structure decay, and it is the
term whose absence from the first Python prototype is discussed in Section 16. The coefficient
χ ≥0 is the conversion of dissipated organization into entropy, in the units used for S, so
that the equations and the prose agree about where lost structure goes. The symbol γ here
is the operational coefficient and corresponds to nothing in the prototype document, whose
own γ multiplies |∇Φ|2 and is written α∇in this specification. The three production terms
are separate mechanisms with separate coefficients, and Section 12 states the rule that keeps
them from counting the same process twice. The equation is a proposed phenomenological form
whose coefficients and units remain to be specified, and it does not inherit an energy-decay
theorem from the prototype. Diffusion acts instantaneously across a connected domain, so these
equations are a local approximation to be run inside causally isolated simulation patches. They
do not enforce the light-cone rule across the galaxy, which needs a separate causal transport
mechanism for the signals between patches.

3.2  The lattice
The browser prototype stores the four component arrays Φ, S, vx, and vy on a 256×256 toroidal
lattice. The torus removes boundary effects, so that the only edges in the world are those
the players and the fields create. The initial player actions are seeding Φ, pumping entropy,
applying shocks, and redirecting flow. These four verbs are the primitive operations from which
every strategic action in Section 11 is built.


                                        9

3.3  Determinism and the branch tree
The field substrate is what makes the time model of Section 2 inexpensive to implement. If the
simulation is deterministic given a seed and a sequence of player interventions, then a player’s
history need only store the interventions along the chosen branches, and any position in the
tree can be recomputed by replaying them from the root. This is the practical meaning of the
statement that only chosen or created branches are calculated. It also fixes a requirement on
the implementation: every source of randomness must be seeded and recorded as part of the
branch. The first Python prototype used unseeded randomness for its scan command, which
would break replay and must be replaced before the time model can be built on it.

3.4  Scopes as organized regions
The nested scopes of Section 4 are the spatial form that organized structure takes in the field
model. A natural reading, adopted here as a design proposal and not a recovered fact, is that a
scope is a region of elevated Φ bounded by a level set, that its boundary is where the constraint
density crosses a threshold, and that the core is the maximum of constraint density within
the region. Popping a scope then corresponds to injecting entropy at the boundary, and the
inward chain reaction corresponds to that entropy being carried along the flow toward the
densest point, where the damage to organization is greatest. On this reading the batteries,
escape routes, and reactors that attract the guide bot are the local maxima of useful structure,
and the core triggers sit near them for the same reason that valuable infrastructure is where a
disruption does the most harm.

4  The World: Scopes, Boundaries, and Cores

4.1  Nested scopes
Space in Entropy’s Edge is organized as nested spheres, which the game calls scopes. A scope
has a boundary, and scopes contain other scopes, so a star system sits inside a larger domain
and contains planets, installations, and fields of its own. The structure is the one used by the
SpherePOP calculus on which the game draws.
  The calculus has a lexical reading that is worth stating, because it explains the vocabulary.
A player fires a crystal by pressing the space bar, t, or y, in the way that a weapon is fired in
Descent. When the crystal has travelled a specified distance it grows into a bubble, and the
bubble corresponds to the opening and closing of parentheses in Racket. Forms such as define,
lambda, and let bind identifiers, the part of a program in which a binding applies is its scope,
and the set of bindings in effect for an expression is its environment. In the game a bubble is
a scope, a player’s environment is the set of bubbles enclosing the ship, and a bubble can be
popped with another crystal or entered without popping by blinking. The ship shrinks as it
moves forward, so that nesting is also a change of scale.

4.2  Popping
Passing through the boundary of a scope pops it. A pop sets off a chain reaction that travels
to the live core of the domain, an innermost nested scope where the trigger resides, along the

                                        10

routing rule stated below. In the ordinary case, in which the core lies inside the crossed scope,
the reaction travels inward. The consequence of a pop is therefore not located at the boundary
that was crossed but at the center of the domain, and it reaches the center after a delay. The
reactor explosion at the end of the game Descent has the same shape: the cause is internal, the
effect travels, and there is a window during which the player can still act.

4.3  The core
The innermost armed scope is called the core. It is the one place where a pop is irreversible.
Outer scopes are forgivable in the sense that the blink mechanism of Section 8 can carry a
player through them without firing anything, but the core cannot be shielded by any tier of
blink. Skill in the game consists largely in reaching and leaving a domain without touching its
core.

4.4  Defusal and relocation
The owner of a domain may deactivate the mechanism in its central scope. Deactivation takes
effect instantly across the scope, and it does not make the domain safe. It changes which scope
is the live core, because the armed state is conserved: when one trigger is retired, another is
created elsewhere in the system. The replacement is not chosen by the owner. It is determined
by relevance, in the manner of a protective boundary that absorbed the first-ranked case so
that the next most probable scenario is activated. The live trigger is therefore the head of a
ranked queue, and defusing removes the head and promotes the runner-up.
   In a simple environment the ranking is legible from the layout. The comparison is the main
breaker of a house: the breaker panel is built so that failures cascade in a known order, and
someone who has wired a building can predict where the next failure goes. In large nested
environments the ranking is only inferable from structure and, where it applies, from traffic,
and reading an environment that nobody has labeled is the upper end of the skill range.
Rule 2 (Conservation of the armed state). At every moment each domain has exactly one live
core. Deactivating it creates another, and an owner cannot place the new core by choice.
Rule 3 (Instant change, delayed observation). A deactivation is instantaneous within the
domain. An observer in another system continues to see the earlier configuration until the
corresponding signal arrives, so a visitor may plan around a trigger that has already been moved.

4.5  Eligibility, queue cycling, and propagation paths
The conservation rule needs a defined domain of application. A domain has a finite set of
eligible scopes, those innermost scopes that can be armed, and the live core is the highest-ranked
eligible scope. Deactivating the core promotes the highest-ranked eligible scope other than the
one retired, which is guaranteed to exist only if the domain has at least two eligible scopes.
A domain with a single eligible scope therefore cannot be defused, and its only core can be
removed only by dismantling the domain. A retired scope is not lost: it re-enters the queue at
the tail after a refractory period, so that repeated defusal cycles through the eligible scopes and
does not exhaust them. A defusal is refused while every other eligible scope is still refractory,
so a domain with two eligible scopes cannot be defused twice in quick succession, and the

                                        11

refusal is reported to the owner as a postponement until a retired scope becomes available
again. Nothing in the rule makes the replacement armed against any particular visitor, since it
is armed only in the sense that it is the live trigger of the domain.
  The specification uses a single routing rule throughout. A domain has exactly one live core,
and a crossing that is not blinked sends a reaction along the unique path in the tree of scopes
from the crossed scope to that core, upward to the lowest common ancestor and then downward.
In the ordinary case the core is a descendant of the crossed scope and the reaction simply travels
inward, and in other cases it first travels outward, so that every unblinked crossing in a domain
reaches the same core. The delay of the reaction grows with the length of the path. This
replaces any rule that chooses among the children of a scope by rank, since a highest-ranked
child need not lead to the live core. The ranking is used only to decide which innermost scope
becomes the live core, with ties broken by a deterministic order that is part of the seed, so that
replay reproduces the same choice. The live core is also the one scope that a blink does not
protect.

5  The Galaxy and Its Contents

5.1 A galaxy built from articles
The stars are named after a curated Wikipedia watchlist, and the structure of each article
furnishes the structure of its star system. The planetary systems are extracted from an article’s
section headings, and the tunnels and surfaces from the content of the corresponding sections.
The recorded example is a star named Free electron model. The geographic zones of its first
planet are named after the first twenty-six words of the article’s first section. The first planetary
system is a planet and its moon, named Ideas and Assumptions, the next system is named
Properties of an electron gas, and so on through the headings. A player who wants to learn
about a subject flies to its star. The galaxy is therefore a map of ideas as well as of matter,
and the difficulty of finding a particular place is the difficulty of finding a particular idea.

5.2  Resources and progression
Level one has three resources, boranium, ironium, and germanium, inherited from Stars! (1995).
Level two adds two more, texture crystals and time crystals. Texture crystals fill in textures
in outline-only zones and allow custom luminosity filters and shaders. Time crystals allow
backward travel in time and act as a vector multiplier, and each time crystal sets the game
back one billion years for all players, so that fourteen of them are needed to set the game back
fourteen billion years without a game over message being issued. One million texture crystals
can be exchanged for one time crystal when none can be found, and the chance that a given
planetary system holds a texture crystal is one in a million, so time crystals are very rare among
level-one players.
   Level two is reached by visiting a fixed number of stars. An earlier record gives the number as
one hundred and fifty thousand and a later one as one hundred thousand, and this specification
treats the count as a parameter N2 with the later figure as its default. At that scale a player
may need years to advance, which is part of the intended difficulty, and fleet automation,
scouting swarms, and programmed waypoints are the means by which the burden of visiting is

                                        12

made bearable.
  A consequence of the stated numbers deserves attention. If every planetary system indepen-
dently has a one-in-a-million chance of a texture crystal, then acquiring fourteen time crystals by
exchange requires fourteen million texture crystals, which is on the order of 1.4 × 1013 systems
in expectation, assuming independent trials, one crystal per successful system, and acquisition
entirely through exchange. It is an expected sampling requirement and not a guaranteed one,
and it is far beyond the 105 stars needed to reach level two. A crystal-funded rewind of the
whole universe is therefore effectively unreachable by ordinary play and is a limit case. Whether
this is intended or the exchange rate should be revisited is recorded as an open question.

5.3  Flares, beacons, and bookmarks
A press of the g key shorter than half a second fires a flare when no acceleration boost is
available, and gives a brief boost when the player is accelerating with the w key. A flare is a
permanent beacon that sticks to walls, glows, and illuminates dark passages and tunnels. It
also sticks to a bubble without popping it. Because it persists, it is a persistent feature of the
world, and it lets a player find the way back out of a deep maze in an asteroid or planet. A
flare fired at a star bookmarks it, so that the star remains visible on the map and when the
view is zoomed out.
  Under the time model of Section 2, a flare belongs to the branch in which it was fired.
Rewinding to a point before the firing removes it from that line of history, and a flare fired on
a branch that is later abandoned remains part of that branch’s record. The permanence of a
flare is a property of a world within a branch and never across branches.

5.4  Removing or enclosing a star
A player who dislikes a particular star may drop a molecular disassembly device into its sun, or
build a minefield or a Dyson sphere around it. The enclosures are treated in Section 9.

5.5  Trajectories as media
Every idea has a force-based location in a global space, in the manner of a word-embedding
space, so that locations correspond to skills or phonological markers. Trajectories flown through
that space at various blink rates correspond to forms of media such as films and music albums.
Certain trajectories are equivalent to, and backward compatible with, flashcard courses and
certain books, so that a player may unlock a trajectory in the vector space by reading a book
or by mastering a deck, in sequence or not, and may do so without a computer. The recorded

7  The G Key and the Global Reset

7.1  Hold time
The g key behaves differently according to how long it is held. A press shorter than half a
second is a tap, which gives a brief acceleration boost to a player who is accelerating and
otherwise fires a flare. A hold longer than half a second but shorter than the reset threshold
th does nothing when released, but it is not silent: an alarm tone builds from the half-second
mark, so that the player is warned before anything irreversible can begin. Reaching th starts
a countdown, with a loud alarm and a flashing warning that the universe will be reset in c
seconds, and releasing the key during the countdown cancels it. Only a key held through the
whole countdown fires the reset. The interval between half a second and one second, which the
first formulation left unspecified, is therefore the warning zone, and the five-second first-use
countdown communicates its warning through sight and sound and not through silence.
  Both quantities shrink as a player accumulates warnings. The threshold th starts at one
second and scales logarithmically toward half a second over many tries, so that eventually any
press beyond a tap enters the countdown. The countdown c starts at five seconds and loses one
second after each warning until it reaches one second. Whether the five seconds of the first
countdown include the threshold interval is a parameter and is left open.

7.2  Three kinds of exposure and protection
The earlier text of this specification used the word inoculation for several different things, and
the review of that text showed that they are not equivalent. Three effects of a reset must be
distinguished.
  The first is temporal exposure. The reset returns the game to the Big Bang, fourteen billion
years back, and the universe unfolds again to the year 2400 over five minutes, on a logarithmic
schedule that is fast at first and slows until it reaches parity with the normal clock. Every
player the reset reaches goes through this, whether or not they lose anything by it.
  The second is loss. A game over is issued to every player who is not blinking when the wave
reaches them, which autoblink makes less likely without guaranteeing. The player’s points are
set to zero, the dictionary of planets visited is wiped, and the names of all planets and stars
are replaced by the words game over for five minutes, which makes some of the minigames
harder. A player who is blinking at the moment the wave arrives is still reset in time but does
not suffer this loss and keeps their points. Enabling autoblink does not by itself provide this,
since the protection requires an actual blink at the moment of arrival, and autoblink serves
by keeping the player blinking often enough that arrival is likely to coincide with one. Super
autoblink gives the same retention whether or not the player happens to be blinking, which is
what distinguishes the two tiers.
  The third is insulation, which is exemption from temporal exposure itself, and it comprises
two properties that must not be confused. Blocking an incoming reset is one property: a
player whose stars lie inside a completed Dyson sphere is invulnerable to resets that reach
them. Preventing a reset from being emitted is the other: an insulating minefield prevents reset
commands from being fired within it, which protects the players outside it and does nothing
for a player inside, who is then contained. The invisibility of a Dyson sphere means that no
further signals from the system escape, so that observers see nothing new from it. It does not
erase light already emitted, and the earlier appearance of the system remains in the skies of
distant observers until later arrivals fail to update it. Neither blink tier provides any of these
properties.

7.3  Propagation and the light cone
The reset spreads outward from its source as a wave at the speed of light. A player is exposed
when the wavefront reaches them and not when the key is pressed, so a distant player learns
of the reset only on arrival, and for such a player the arrival is at once the warning and the
event. This respects the rule that no information about another player’s present can travel
faster than light. In particular, super autoblink can respond to the arrival of the wave but
cannot respond to its emission, because responding to the emission would require information
that the multiplayer rules of Section 10 forbid. The recorded statement that the reset applies
to all players is therefore read as applying to all players the wave reaches.

7.4  Disincentives
The reset is surrounded by disincentives, and the design hopes that no one ever holds the key
that long. The location of the player who presses it is broadcast to the other players. The
nearest players may build an insulating minefield or a Dyson swarm around the offender’s stars
and planets, which inoculates them against that player’s reset and contains the source. The
offender’s points are set to zero and the dictionary of visited planets is wiped. Players are asked
to be respectful of newcomers, and the advice to everyone is to enable autoblink as soon as
they begin to play.
  The mechanism has the form of what the Kalabari call a counterfoil choice, in which one
option is offered chiefly to show where the decision should not go. The reset is the empty bowl:
it is placed next to a useful action on the same key, its alarm shows the player where the choice
leads, and the design depends on the norms of the community that the display is meant to
reinforce and not on prohibition.

7.5  Crystal-funded rewinds
The recorded rule is that each time crystal sets the game back one billion years for all players,
and that fourteen of them set the game back fourteen billion years without a game over message.
The specification reads this as a reset financed by resources, in which the loss of the preceding
kind is not issued, so that it is the considerate alternative to holding the key. Whether temporal
exposure still applies to other players is not stated, and the exchange numbers make the full
rewind a limit case, as noted in Section 5.

7.6  Heat death and the annual cycle
An earlier version of the design had the calendar reset to 2400 every January 1, because someone
always triggers a runaway heat death on December 31, as the trigger mechanism of interstellar
mines becomes more sensitive with time. A player who is a grabby alien, having visited every
star in the observable universe long before that date, simply waits for it. The specification


                                        17

proposes a reconciliation with the rest of the time model, and it remains a proposal until the
designer adopts it.
  The proposal treats January 1 as an annual scenario boundary, while the Big Bang reset
remains an event inside a scenario. The two mechanics then do not compete for control of one
clock. The annual cycle follows the real-world calendar in a declared server timezone. Each
annual scenario begins with the displayed year at 2400, and players then advance, rewind, and
suffer resets under the rules already stated. January 1 starts a new scenario identifier and
does not rewind the previous scenario. The completed scenario and its branch histories are
archived, so that neither provenance nor observations are erased. The causal coordinate τ of
Section 2 continues to increase across the transition, and the scenario identifier records which
environment an event belongs to.
  Under this reading the December 31 heat death is a terminal environmental process whose
hazard rises with the age of the scenario. A player-triggered Big Bang reset changes the
displayed cosmological year and does not lower that hazard or restart the annual schedule,
since otherwise repeated resets could postpone the annual ending indefinitely. The five-minute
unfolding belongs to Big Bang resets only, and the January transition initializes the next
scenario at 2400 directly.
  The annual transition is an engine rule and not a wave emitted somewhere in the galaxy.
Players may know its schedule in advance without learning anything about another player’s
present. Heat-death disturbances inside the closing scenario still obey causal propagation, but
the scheduled retirement of the scenario does not need to masquerade as a physical signal.
Dyson insulation therefore protects against reset waves within a scenario and does not prevent
the scenario from ending.
   Events retain their scenario identifier and remain attached to that scenario’s histories.
A signal still in flight at the annual boundary becomes an archived pending event.  It can
arrive if that history is later resumed and cannot enter the next scenario, which keeps the
branch-assignment rule intact and prevents an old reset wave from striking a newly initialized
universe.
  The default proposed for what carries between scenarios is the player’s archive, learned
controls, accessibility settings, and historical achievements, together with a fresh strategic state.
Whether visited-star knowledge or earned resources also carry over is a separate progression
decision that the annual-clock rule does not settle. In summary, a reset restarts cosmological
development within a recorded history, and January 1 starts another annual scenario while
preserving the record of the previous one.

global reset, and the recorded rationale is that the reset is the only way to reach extra-ocular
regions, those outside the particle horizon. The mechanism by which a reset opens such regions

8  Blink, Autoblink, and Super Autoblink

8.1  Blink
The b key blinks. A blink refreshes the visuals when there are too many texture tracers and
Sobel edges on screen, it allows the player to enter a bubble without popping it, and it allows
the player to rotate without changing the contrast when pressed together with q or e. Because
outlines grow thicker and blurrier over time, a player who is not moving should blink about
every five seconds or move. In the design’s own terms, blinking is correct traversal: it is how a
boundary is crossed without firing it.

8.2  Autoblink
Holding a and b together enables autoblink, which blinks automatically when necessary. It
covers the outer scopes and does not protect the core. It prevents a player from accidentally
popping bubbles while moving through nested space, and it keeps the player blinking often
enough that a reset wave is likely to arrive in the middle of a blink, which is why the notes
describe it as increasing the chances of not losing progress and not as guaranteeing them.
Experienced players keep it on almost continuously, so it functions as a filter that separates
brand-new players from those who have learned the traversal and grants little power beyond
that. The design describes the relationship in two phrases: blinking is correct traversal, and
autoblink is delegated traversal, in which the player automates their own correct crossing. Early
formulations wrote the activation as a followed by b, and the specification fixes the chord as
canonical, with the input rules of Section 6 governing it.

8.3  Super autoblink
Pressing s, then a, then b enables super autoblink. It blinks automatically when passing through
an outer scope and also when the reset wave arrives at the player’s location, so that retention
does not depend on timing. It is the unconditional tier, and the ordered sequence is meant to
make it harder to enable by accident and to read as a layer stacked on top of autoblink.
  Super autoblink also adds perception. While it is enabled the player sees an amber warning
on the areas that will set off triggers, and specifically on the armed innermost scopes that no
blink tier protects. The overlay shows the armed configuration that is locally observable to the
player. A change made elsewhere appears only after its signal arrives, so that the overlay never
reveals the remote configuration earlier than the light-cone rules allow, and within the player’s
own domain it updates at once when a core is deactivated and replaced.

9  Minefields, Containment, and Salvage

The bomb key drops a mine and is to be used only for extraplanetary minefields. Mining is a
deliberate action with its own binding and is not a side effect of any other mechanic. Each
mine is a domain consisting of a single armed scope, so every mine is its own live core and
cannot be relocated, and a minefield is a set of such domains. The alternative reading, in which
a field is one domain with exactly one live mine at a time, yields a different game in which
defusing a mine promotes another, and it is recorded as a variant. The base specification uses
the first reading because it matches the salvage economy below, in which a mine is removed by
being scrapped and not by being moved.

9.1  Containment and insulation
A minefield has two roles, which the transcripts record. It contains a player who has announced
their location by holding the reset key, since a field built around their stars and planets means
they cannot easily leave. It also insulates the builders, because a field prevents reset commands
from being fired within it, so that the players who build it are inoculated against the offender’s
key. The nearest players do this, and the farther players are protected by their distance and by
the delay of the wave.

9.2  Dyson spheres and swarms
Dyson swarms and spheres serve two purposes. The nearest players build swarms around an
offender’s system to protect the rest of the galaxy. Advanced players build spheres around their
own systems because they do not wish to reset the universe for others, and a completed sphere
makes a star invisible to other players and invulnerable to resets. A sphere is not built in real
time by the player. The player sets up the infrastructure by selecting a suitable technology tree
and setting the factory defaults correctly, and the completed sphere is visible only far in the

                                        20

future, so that a player must travel a long way forward in time to see it finished. A player who
wants to experiment with the reset can build one around their own system.

9.3  Hidden until tested
A trapped player does not learn of a minefield until they try to leave their solar system. There
is no notification, and a player who has announced their location with the reset and then lives
quietly for years cannot tell whether a fence was built around them. The absence of information
is part of the cost of announcing.

9.4 Who is caught
A well-placed mine does not rely on outer scopes, because autoblinkers cross those cleanly. Its
value lies in where the core trigger sits relative to the route out of the system. A minefield is
therefore a bet about which path a trapped player will take, and a counter-bet is available in
super autoblink, whose amber overlay shows the armed cores and thus the field, as far as the
player’s own light cone reveals it. Newcomers and players without perception are caught, and
experienced players with the top tier are warned.

9.5  Salvage
A mined player is not trapped permanently. Once the minelayer owns skimmers, the field
can be scrapped for resources. The mines are capital and the scrap is the return, which gives
other players a reason to mine a system that has nothing to do with hostility toward its
occupant. Containment is an investment with a payoff schedule, and the length of a player’s
confinement depends on someone else’s progression. Fleet infrastructure supports the work:
mass accelerators and starbases build drone scouts, miners, mine-layers, and transports, and
waypoints with repeating orders allow resource distribution networks to be programmed, so
that salvage can be carried out by fleets sent ahead.
Rule 4 (Retirement without removal). Because deactivation relocates the live core and does not
remove it, the owner of a nested installation with several eligible scopes may retire its armed
state by shifting the trigger to another scope while leaving the old layout looking armed. A
player who passes through a deactivated installation may never learn whether it was dangerous.
Single-scope mines are not subject to this rule, since they have nowhere to move their trigger.

10  Multiplayer: Isolation and Light-Cone Verification

10.1  Scattered players
Players are scattered so far apart that they cannot influence each other directly. Each player’s
tree of choices is private, so there is no shared timeline to keep consistent and nothing to
reconcile. Two players who are both at the year 2400 are not at the same time in any sense they
can check, because there is no event that both could observe. A year is a coordinate within
one’s own tree, and the phrase when amounts to how many of one’s own choices deep one is.


                                        21

10.2  Travel as verification
Interaction is possible, but it is paid for in travel time. A player who travels to another player
twenty-six thousand light years away must spend twenty-six thousand years of travel to arrive,
and cannot see what the other player is doing now. What the traveler can see is the implication
of the other player’s choices as they have propagated: the consequences that the signal has had
time to carry. The player sees effects and not claims.
   This inverts the defect that motivated the design. On the social platform, a stranger’s date is
a label the reader must trust. Here, a stranger’s date can only be inferred from the downstream
evidence of their choices, which is far harder to forge than a field, and the cost of seeing it is
time actually spent.

10.3  Deniable presence
Visibility is gated by causal effect. A visit leaves no mark on the visited player unless that
player’s choices carry consequences into the future the visitor travels to, and even then what
registers is the consequence, not the visitor. The record of a visit exists only in the visitor’s
own tree. Presence is deniable by default, in the way that a night sky never tells you who is
looking at it but only what the light from you did. A player whose choices have no downstream
effects is permanently invisible to everyone, and quiet play is a legitimate way to stay unseen.
The global reset is the one deliberate exception, since it announces the location of whoever
triggers it.

10.4  Rewrites and what observers see
An observation made across distance is true of the state that was committed when the signal
left. A later revision by the observed player, made by projected inquiry and interpolation, forks
from that point, and the observer’s view stays true of the branch they saw. The observer learns
of the revision only when its own signal arrives. Abandoned branches therefore persist in the
observer’s record as something that really happened to the version of the other player that they
observed.

10.5  Event transmission and branch assignment
Isolation postpones the problem of consistency between private histories but does not remove
it. A visitor can observe a branch, act on what was observed, and send an effect back, and
the specification needs an explicit rule for which branch receives that effect. Each transmitted
event is therefore recorded with four parts: the origin branch, meaning the node in the sender’s
tree at which it was emitted; the emission coordinate in space and time; the destination; and
the arrival condition, which is the light-travel delay together with any further condition the
event carries.
  An event is delivered to a branch of the recipient’s tree if and only if its arrival condition
is met on that branch. A reply to an event is addressed to the emission node of the event it
answers, and it is delivered to every branch in the original sender’s tree that contains that node
among its ancestors, inclusive. A branch that was forked from a point before the emission does
not receive it, because on that branch the original event was never sent. Rewinding does not

                                        22

retract an event already in flight. Pending arrivals remain attached to the branches from which
they were emitted, so that a message sent on an abandoned line continues to travel and to
arrive as a fact about that line, and a new branch, if it wishes to send a message, emits its
own. A player who rewinds therefore cannot erase what has already left, but can ensure that
its consequences fall on a version of themselves they no longer inhabit, and a player who later
returns to the abandoned branch by cheap forward replay will find the replies that arrived there
in the meantime. The rule is the one that keeps the observer’s account true: what someone
observed was real on the branch they observed, and the answer they sent is addressed to that
same branch.
  Incoming events must also be part of the replay record. A computed node cannot be
reproduced from its seed and the player’s interventions alone if an external reply is later inserted
into its past. When a new arrival would alter an already computed stretch, the stretch is
preserved and a new continuation is created that incorporates the arrival. An inactive branch
can hold a pending event without being simulated, and when it is resumed it advances to the
arrival, applies it, and only then computes later states. Replay is therefore unchanged only as
far as the earliest external event that newly applies to it.
  The scheduling coordinate for arrivals is the causal coordinate τ of Section 2, and the engine
keeps a hidden correspondence between the causal coordinates of different players, which players
never see.

11  The Strategic Layer

11.1  The four activities reinterpreted
The four conventional activities of a 4X game receive interpretations drawn from the field
substrate. Exploration is the discovery of gradients and of useful field configurations, so a
map is a record of where organization is cheap to maintain and where it is not. Expansion is
the seeding of constraints that can persist, which is a different thing from claiming territory,
because a seeded region that the dissipation term overwhelms is lost without any opponent
acting. Exploitation is the capture of flows and the export of entropy. Warfare includes injecting
entropy into an opponent’s structures and disrupting the conditions that support them, so that
the weapon of choice is often an attack on the environment and not on the occupant.

11.2  Infrastructure
The design names four kinds of infrastructure: Autocatalytic Nodes, Constraint Builders,
Entropy Pumps, and Memory Crystals. The names were proposed in the design discussion, and
the record does not establish that all of them became functioning objects, so the roles below
are stated as the natural field-level reading and not as recovered specifications. A Constraint
Builder is a source of Φ, the term σΦ in Section 3. An Entropy Pump is the export term π.
An Autocatalytic Node is a source whose output grows with the local value of Φ, so that a
well-maintained region reinforces itself and a neglected one loses its reinforcement. A Memory
Crystal is a structure that preserves organization against dissipation, and its role in the time
model remains to be decided: the consumable time crystals that slow the passage of time share
part of the name, and the two may be the same object or related ones.

                                        23

11.3  Stars, corridors, and fleets
Star systems are the nodes of the strategic map. Each star samples the local values of Φ, S, and
v, and those samples determine its character. Corridors are connected regions of low entropy,
detected from the field, and they are the routes along which a civilization can maintain contact
with its settlements. Travel cost depends on distance, on entropy along the route, and on
corridor modifiers. Mass accelerators and starbases are the hubs of this network, and starbases
build the drone scouts, miners, mine-layers, and transports that carry out its work. Fleets follow
waypoints with repeating orders, which lets a player program resource distribution networks
for the three level-one resources, and the orders may be conditional, for example mining one
resource only while a stockpile is below a given fraction. Colonization requires a habitable star
that nobody owns. The result is a geography in which routes and settlement opportunities
depend partly on conditions that the players can themselves alter, and overextension arises
from the simulated conditions: a civilization that spreads beyond what its corridors can keep
organized loses the outlying settlements to dissipation without an enemy being involved.
   Fleet movement and colonization were chosen as the next development step after the economy,
the star-system nodes, and corridor detection, and that sequence of decisions is a fixed point
of the plan. One consequence of the light-cone rules of Section 10 requires attention. Travel
between distant players takes as many years as there are light years of separation, so corridor
modifiers can change the cost of a journey, in energy or in entropy exposure, but cannot shorten
its duration below the light-travel time without contradicting the isolation of players. This
specification therefore treats corridors as modifiers of cost and not of speed.

11.4  Factions
Five factions were proposed: the Lamphron Ascetics, the Lamphrodyne Industrialists, the
Vectic Nomads, the Crystal Archivists, and the Parasite Syndicates. Their names suggest
different relationships to organization and flow, an ascetic discipline of constraint, an industrial
throughput, a life carried on the flow, a custody of stored structure, and a dependence on the
organization of others, but the recovered record does not contain their original descriptions,
bonuses, or histories. Those are open design work, and this specification does not supply them.

11.5  Victory conditions and progression
Four victory conditions were proposed: Persistent Constraint, Entropy Mastery, Flow Dominion,
and Reintegration. The envisioned progression runs from vulnerable islands of organization,
through conflict over corridors, toward the stabilization of structure at galactic scale. Other
proposals from the same discussion include research organized around Constraint Regimes,
dynamic entropy events, artificial opponents whose objectives are expressed through Lyapunov-
style criteria, and multiplayer diplomacy built on a shared entropy environment.
  The last of these conflicts with the isolation of players in Section 10, and the conflict needs a
provisional resolution. Players cannot share a field that all of them can see and alter, because
no signal crosses between them faster than light. The shared entropy environment can instead
be understood as the sum of delayed contributions: at any moment, the entropy a player
experiences from the rest of the galaxy is the accumulated effect of what the others did,
arriving after the appropriate delay. Diplomacy in such a world is conducted entirely through

consequences that arrive late, which agrees with the principle that what players learn about
each other is effect and never claim.

12.1  Field ontology and the variational form

14  Visual Direction

The visual language has two recoverable components. The simulation design calls for scalar
heatmaps, luminous vector filaments, crystalline regions where entropy is low, and distorted
regions where it is high, so that the physical state of the world is visible and a player can
read the health of a civilization from the look of its surroundings. The second component is a
direction given for the ships and the general styling: retro styling with futuristic ships, and

  Two features of the mechanics fit this direction naturally. The amber warning that super
autoblink places on armed cores belongs to the vocabulary of retro instrument displays, the
amber phosphor of old terminals, and so reads as part of the same world and not as an
overlay laid on top. The attract mode of the guide bot is also a retro form, the self-running
demonstration of an arcade cabinet, and it gives the world a reason to look the way it does.
  The most difficult feature of the display is that objects are shown in outline only, in the
manner of a vector outline or a Sobel filter. The edges are green when near and orange when
distant, and they grow thicker and blurrier over time, so that a player who is not moving must
blink about every five seconds or move, or enable autoblink. The player rotates the world’s

already tripped, or repeats the same mistake each time it replays an environment. The choice
affects how long a given tutorial environment remains instructive.

16  Implementation Status and Roadmap

16.1 What exists
The browser prototype described in the design discussion is organized as an HTML page, a main
script, and a simulation script, followed by scripts for stars, corridors, fleets, and movement,
with optional Python support for persistence and batch parameter sweeps. These are records
of code supplied or described in conversation, and they do not establish that a particular build
is running today.
  The most recent concrete implementation is a small turn-based Python model of about
forty lines, with typed commands and a state consisting of the turn number, energy, entropy,
buildings, and tiles. Each turn changes energy and entropy by

               ∆E = 1 + 2f,   ∆S = 0.2f + 0.05 ℓ,
where f is the number of factories and ℓthe number of laboratories. A factory costs 5 energy
and a laboratory costs 4. With two factories and one laboratory, starting from 10 energy, ten
turns with no intervening purchases yield 60 energy and an entropy increase of 4.5. The scan
command generates tiles with unseeded randomness and does not affect these projections.

16.2  The gap
The principal limitation of that model is that entropy accumulates without feeding back into
production, construction, or survival. Under the tested building policy, growth is therefore
unchecked. This is a limitation of the model’s adequacy and not an implementation bug, but it
is also the largest distance between the prototype and the design, because the design makes
maintaining organization consequential and the prototype records entropy without imposing
any consequence for it.

The smallest change that closes the gap is to make entropy act on the three things it should
govern. Production becomes ∆Eeff = (1 + 2f) g(S), where g is a decreasing function with
g(0) = 1, such as g(S) = 1/(1+S/S0) for a scale S0 to be tuned. Construction cost is multiplied
by an increasing function c(S) of the same quantity. Existing structures acquire a per-turn
hazard h(S) of degrading or being lost, which is the discrete counterpart of the dissipation term

balanced economy is sustainable and a regime in which unchecked expansion collapses. Whether
it actually has them depends on the coefficients, on the cost and capacity of pumps, and on
what counts as collapse, and the equations do not by themselves establish either outcome.
The statements that a factory-only policy fails and that a policy including pumps survives are
therefore experimental acceptance targets, to be demonstrated by running the model, and they
are not claims about the model.

18  Open Questions

Several decisions remain open and are recorded here so that they are settled deliberately and
not by default. Whether the relevance ranking is computed from observed traffic through a
system or from the structure of the nesting alone determines whether dangerous areas drift
toward the busiest routes. Whether a hit on a mine destroys something or only stops the
player and reveals the field determines whether the cost of discovery arrives before or after
the knowledge. Whether the amber overlay shows only the boundaries that would fire on the
player, or also the runner-up in the ranking, determines how much of the hidden order a super
autoblinker can read. Whether auto blink can be tied to early detection of mines is a possible
extension. Whether a mine respects blink in the same way a sphere boundary does remains
unstated in the design notes, and this specification adopts the working assumption that mines
are cores in the sense of Section 4 and are therefore not covered by any tier, while outer scopes
of a field are.
  The addition of the strategic layer opens further questions. The equations of the field
substrate are a candidate form, and the coefficients and the flow-reorientation rule remain to
be fixed by experiment. The faction descriptions and the full set of victory conditions are
unspecified beyond their names. It is undecided whether time crystals and Memory Crystals
are one object. It is undecided whether the entropy hazard h(S) applies uniformly or depends
on the type of structure, and whether the relevance ranking of Section 4 can be computed from
the field, for instance as a function of Φ and the flow through each scope, so that the live core
drifts toward the busiest and most organized regions without any separate rule. The pairing of
a turn-based layer with a real-time layer raises the question of how many flight-layer seconds
correspond to a year, and whether the guide bot’s attract mode runs in the flight layer, the
strategic layer, or both.
  The records leave further matters unsettled. The count of stars needed for level two is given
as one hundred thousand in a later record and one hundred and fifty thousand in an earlier
one. The exchange rate of one million texture crystals for one time crystal, together with
the one-in-a-million chance of finding one, makes a fourteen-crystal rewind a limit case that
requires on the order of 1013 systems, and it is unclear whether that is intended. It is unclear
whether the countdown of the first reset warning includes the threshold interval. What carries
between annual scenarios beyond the archive and settings is undecided. The typing tutor at
the center of each star has no stated relation to the core trigger, and it is unclear whether
arriving at a core through inept flight leads to the tutor or to the reaction. It is unclear whether
the g of command mode is the lowercase or the uppercase key of Vim. The mapping from
particular books, decks, and media to trajectories in the global space is unspecified. Whether a
crystal-funded rewind still exposes other players to temporal exposure is unspecified, and so is
the mechanism by which a reset reaches the extra-ocular regions beyond the particle horizon.
Finally, the correct reading of a minefield as many single-scope domains or as one domain with
a single live mine has been decided here in favor of the former, and the other reading remains
available as a variant.

19  Relation to the Originating Problem

The social-platform defect that prompted the design can be restated in the vocabulary of this
specification. A single date field serves as both the platform’s record and the poster’s claim,
so there is no distinction between a position reached by ordinary advance and one reached by
an unpriced jump. Backdating is permitted for legitimate reasons, such as digitizing family
photographs, but nothing marks a backdated item as the poster’s assertion, and nothing keeps it
from feeding the signals by which readers judge credibility. Entropy’s Edge supplies the missing
structure: moves along the date axis are priced, the record of how a position was reached is kept
apart from the position itself, interpolated stretches are marked, hidden structure is revealed to
those who pay to see it, and what travels between parties is consequence. These are offered as
design properties of a game and as an illustration of what a date field would look like if the
seams were drawn on it.
